html:
The Volga is the longest river in Europe, about 3,500 km long. It rises in the hills northwest of Moscow, flows east and then south through the heart of Russia, and empties into the Caspian Sea at Astrakhan.

For a thousand years it was a highway between the forests of the north and the Islamic world:

  • The Khazars had their capital, Itil, near its mouth.
  • The Volga Bulgars grew rich on its middle course trading furs, slaves and silver. Ibn Fadlan visited them in 922 and described the Rus traders he met there.
  • The Mongol Golden Horde ruled from Sarai on its lower course.

Its successor states, the Kazan and Astrakhan khanates, fell to Ivan the Terrible in 1552 and 1556, and the whole river became Russian. The Nizhny Novgorod Fair grew where the Oka joins it. Catherine the Great invited German farmers to its lower valley in 1763.

The river also saw hunger and war: the famine of 1921 hit the Volga region worst, and the battle of Stalingrad was fought on its banks in 1942 and 1943. Soviet dams turned much of it into a chain of reservoirs.
